HomeStyle Retailers - Q2 2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the HomeStyle Retailers Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, during the Q&A session, please limit yourself to one question and one follow-up. Please also note, today's event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations:
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, and thank you for joining us today to discuss HomeStyle Retailers' results for the Q2 2024. Joining me on today’s call are Mark Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer; and David Ruiz, Chief Merchandising Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements, which are subject to risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

With that, I’ll turn the call over to Mark Thompson.

Mark Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you, Sarah. Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I’m pleased to report HomeStyle Retailers' performance for the Q2 2024. We continued to execute on our strategic priorities and delivered solid results despite the challenging macroeconomic environment.

Today I will cover five key aspects of our performance. First, our sales per square foot reached new highs, reflecting improved store productivity. Second, while e-commerce growth remained steady through omnichannel channels like BOPIS, it supported overall traffic. Third, store performance showed resilience with optimized space and category strength. Fourth, our marketing initiatives, including loyalty programs, drove meaningful engagement. And fifth, supply chain optimization delivered significant efficiencies.

We are confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value for our shareholders.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Lisa Chen to provide more details on our financial results.

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Thank you, Mark. Good morning. I'll provide a more detailed review of our financial performance for the Q2 2024. Our total revenue for the quarter was $2.75 billion, a 4.5% increase compared to the same period last year, driven by comparable store sales growth of 4.2%. Gross margin came in at 37.9%, reflecting a 130 basis point decline primarily from elevated markdown activity, though offset somewhat by procurement savings and occupancy leverage. Operating expenses were $1.03 billion, representing 37.5% of revenue, as we continued to invest prudently in store remodels and digital capabilities while holding SG&A flat as a percentage. Net income was $138 million, or $0.92 per share. We generated $280 million in cash flow from operations, supporting share repurchases and debt reduction. Inventory levels are currently well-controlled at $2.1 billion, equivalent to 14.2 weeks of supply, down from 15.1 weeks last year.

We are maintaining a strong balance sheet and are well positioned to invest in our growth initiatives.

To give more color on the operational drivers behind these results, let me expand on the key metrics Mark highlighted, starting with sales per square foot, one of our most critical KPIs in the brick-and-mortar space. Sales per square foot, or SPSF, is net retail sales divided by average selling square footage, excluding non-revenue areas like backrooms and offices. It's the benchmark for store productivity and asset efficiency, especially with real estate costs eating up 8-12% of sales and leases being long-term commitments—a small 1-2% improvement here translates to real ROIC gains.

On a trailing 12-month basis, company-wide SPSF hit $528 per square foot, a 4.8% rise year-over-year from $504, our best since pre-pandemic 2019 at $515. Quarter-over-quarter, Q2 LTM SPSF gained 2.1% from Q1's $517, thanks to summer categories like outdoor living and decor. For Q2 comp stores, SPSF was $132 per square foot, up 5.2% from $125 last year, beating our 3.8% comp sales growth due to our selling square footage optimization, trimming 7% of non-productive space with micro-fulfillment and better fixtures. This positions us ahead of Macy's at around $310 LTM and Kohl's at $380, and narrowing the gap to leaders like Williams-Sonoma at $1,200 or Best Buy at $950.

Regionally, our hyper-local approach shines through. Northeast urban stores in Boston and NYC led at $615 LTM SPSF, up 6.7% year-over-year, boosted by mall traffic recovery and shop-in-shop artisan partnerships. The South, 42% of our space, reached $525, plus 4.1%, riding Texas and Florida migration with 12% traffic gains in suburban centers. West Coast trailed at $485, up 3.2%, hit by California tourism softness and wildfires, but pop-up events like REI's are helping.

By category, home furnishings drove 62% of the gain to $680 SPSF, up 7.3%, led by TikTok-viral modular shelving. Appliances up 4.9% to $450 as shortages eased. Softlines like bedding grew just 1.8% to $380 amid inventory issues, but AI dynamic pricing is tackling that.

Post-COVID shifts to destination stores helped, with BOPIS now 28% of store sales, up from 19%, aided by 3.2 points from higher average selling prices despite trade-downs. Comps adjust for last year's Midwest weather hit.

Initiatives include closing 14 low performers under $400 SPSF, remodeling 85 with RFID planograms cutting out-of-stocks 22% and lifting sell-through 11%, adding $18 per square foot. We reallocated 15% to hero zones like Home Depot's buying walls for 9% uplift, used SpaceIQ analytics for adjacencies boosting cross-sell 14%, and sustainability upgrades like LEDs saving $2 per square foot in OpEx.

Ahead, we aim for $560 LTM by fiscal 2025 via compact 12,000 square foot pilots targeting $750 like Urban Outfitters, exclusive Yeti and Dyson zones for 6-8% premium, and AR mirrors for 5% conversion like Sephora. Risks like sunbelt taxes are manageable with 72% owned properties.

Next, markdown activity and its margin impact. Markdowns rose to 14.8% of net sales, up 210 basis points from 12.7% last year, pressuring gross margin to 37.9% from 39.2%. Ex-markdowns, merchandise margin was steady at 41.2% with good vendor deals on cotton and freight. Shrink ticked to 1.8% from 1.6% due to urban crime.

Drivers were higher starting inventory, weak spring sell-through, and clearance for fall. Inventory up 8% to $2.1 billion but weeks improved to 14.2. Cool weather hurt apparel and patio in Northeast/Midwest, 45% of footprint, with apparel units per transaction down 3%.

Sun Belt markdowns at 11.5%, down 50 basis points on tourism and back-to-school. Midwest/Northeast hit 18.2%, up from 14.9%, with garden centers needing 25-40% off. Markdowns peaked at 16.5% mid-quarter but fell to 13.2% by June, better than Q1's 15.4%, targeting 13-14% full year—better than Macy's 16.1% or Kohl's 17.3%. Turns hit 3.8x from 3.5x.

Tools include RetailFlow AI with Blue Yonder, up 22% forecast accuracy, cutting overbuys 15%; RFID at 75% in apparel; smart shelves auto-discounting slow movers. Private labels at 28% have 40% less markdowns with JIT from Bangladesh. Vendor scorecards recovered $25 million; district markdown authority improved margins 5% in tests.

Q3 markdowns seen at 13.5%, gross margin 38.0-38.5% with comps leverage. Risks: spending caution, tariffs.

Turning to traffic versus average ticket breakdown for our 4.2% comp sales, outpacing sector's flat traffic. Traffic rose 1.8%, ticket 2.3% to $48.72—balanced, improving from Q1's 0.9%/2.5%.

Traffic: 1.8% growth or 2.3 million weekly visitors via Placer.ai and sensors. BOPIS 28% of digital drove 15% store traffic; ship-from-store 8%. Rewards app up 12% loyalty traffic; geo-fencing spiked weekends 22%. Remodels (40% fleet) up 5.2% traffic, dwell 24 minutes with AR kiosks.

Sunbelt +3.4%, Northeast +0.5%, Midwest +2.1%, Canada +1.2%.

Ticket: Apparel AUR up 3.1% on private labels +14%; home bundling +4.2%. Conversion 32%, add-ons 11% via AI devices. Categories: essentials +1.5%, discretionary +3.8%.

Validates stores-first: RFID cuts stockouts 22%. Q3: traffic +2.5%, ticket +2.0% with remodels.

On regional variations for our 4.8% comps across 1,250 stores. Northeast (28%) +6.2% on traffic +3.1%, ticket $128, home demand; BOPIS lockers +15% comps. Margins +90 bps to 42.1%.

Southeast (32%) +7.1%, traffic +4.7%, outdoor +14%; turns 5.2x. Midwest (22%) +2.9%, ticket $112 offsets flat traffic; AI planograms +8% productivity. West (18%) -0.3%, ticket $132 premium but wildfires, wages; remodels for H2 lift.

Sunbelt/urban lead; adjusted comps +5.6%. BOPIS 22% sales, turns 5.1x.

Finally, supply chain efficiencies: DIO 52 days from 68, turns 7.0x beating Target/Walmart. Costs 6.2% sales, down 110 bps; freight -12% to 4.1%, OOS 3.2%.

West DCs 97% on-time via Mexico nearshoring. Europe Rotterdam cuts delays; Asia yen savings.

Supply Chain 2.0: $250M AI forecasting 92% accurate, safety stock -22%; automation 85% DCs, picking +35%; RFID 70% cuts shrink 0.8%; TMS +11% savings.

Stores as micro-DCs: 75% same-day BOPIS, 18% sales. Emissions -22%. FY25: 8-10% cuts, DIO <50.

These underpin 30 bps Op margin expansion.

Now, I'd like to hand it over to David Ruiz, our Chief Merchandising Officer, to discuss our new product lines.

David Ruiz, Chief Merchandising Officer:
Thank you, Lisa. This quarter, we launched our EcoHome sustainable living line, which has seen exceptional early traction with 25% sell-through above plan in the first month, particularly in modular furnishings and energy-efficient appliances. Initial feedback highlights strong resonance with eco-conscious shoppers, contributing over 2% to comp sales in test stores. We are excited about the potential of this new product and other upcoming launches like expanded outdoor collections for holiday.

Now, let's open the line for questions.

Operator:
Thank you. As a reminder, please limit to one question and one follow-up. Our first question comes from John Smith with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Smith (Goldman Sachs):
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the impact of inflation on your sales?

Mark Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Good morning, John. Inflation remains a mixed bag—higher average selling prices added about 3.2 points to key metrics like SPSF, but we've seen some trade-down to value tiers, which our essentials and private labels have captured well. Our traffic acceleration and basket-building offset this, keeping comps positive.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Davis with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Emily Davis (JPMorgan):
What are your expectations for same-store sales growth in the next quarter?

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Thanks, Emily. We're guiding to 3-5% comp sales growth for Q3, with traffic around 2.5% on back-to-school and early holiday, and continued ticket strength from assortment productivity and remodels. Markdowns easing to 13.5% will support margins.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Mike Patel with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Mike Patel (Barclays):
Can you elaborate on the supply chain improvements?

Mark Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Absolutely, Mike. Our Supply Chain 2.0 investments cut DIO to 52 days and boosted turns to 7.0x through AI forecasting at 92% accuracy, warehouse robotics lifting picking 35%, and RFID visibility reducing shrink to 0.8%. Nearshoring and TMS optimizations kept costs down 110 basis points despite disruptions, fueling availability and comps.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Laura Chen with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Laura Chen (Morgan Stanley):
On margins, how sustainable is the markdown pressure relief?

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Good question, Laura. Q3 gross margin should land 38.0-38.5%, with markdowns at 13.5% thanks to RetailFlow AI improving forecasts 22%, higher private label penetration at 28% with lower markdown incidence, and vendor clawbacks. Full-year, we see deleveraging offset by supply chain savings and comp leverage.

Operator:
Thank you. That concludes the question-and-answer session. I'll now turn the call back over to Mark Thompson for closing remarks.

Mark Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, we are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our long-term strategy. Thank you for your continued support.

Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations:
This concludes today's call. Thank you for joining us.
